title: Why do we carve pumpkins at Halloween? It began with a turnip

sources.name: National Museum of Ireland — Ghost turnip, collection F1943.350
Clemson Cooperative Extension (2023) — The origins of the jack-o’-lantern

practice: Try another small surprise from the past in the History Quiz.

sections.html:
Halloween pumpkin carving developed from an Irish tradition of making lanterns from turnips. The pumpkin version took shape in North America, where pumpkins were available and became the familiar orange face of Halloween.

So the pumpkin got the starring role. A rather alarming root vegetable did some of the earlier work.
sections.title: Before the pumpkin

sections.html:
The National Museum of Ireland’s ghost turnip records the older custom. In 1943, a teacher sent the museum a turnip lantern from County Donegal, explaining that people there had made that type around 1900.

The display object is a painted plaster model made by museum artist Eileen Barnes. It is not a vegetable that somehow stayed fresh for a century.
sections.title: A clue in a museum

sections.html:
One Irish tale retold by Clemson Extension follows Stingy Jack, a trickster refused entry to both Heaven and Hell. He wanders with a glowing ember inside a hollow turnip.

That is folklore, not the biography of a proven lantern inventor. It explains the name jack-o’-lantern through a story with an excellent spooky prop.
sections.title: Who was Jack?

sections.html:
Irish immigrants carried their traditions to North America, where pumpkins offered another way to make the lantern. The custom changed materials as it travelled.

That makes the smiling pumpkin a small story about migration as well as Halloween. Next, discover why another familiar Halloween ritual begins with the words “trick or treat”.
sections.title: An orange change of cast

description: Before Halloween pumpkins, there were turnip lanterns. Meet the Irish ghost story and the much less cheerful vegetable behind the jack-o’-lantern.
